title: Responsible AI and Ethics
summary: As AI makes decisions affecting people's lives, building it responsibly is not optional. Models can inherit and amplify bias from data, leading to unfair outcomes. Explainability tools like SHAP and LIME help you understand why a model made a decisio
content:
# Responsible AI and Ethics ##### The hiring model that learned to reject women In 2014 Amazon built a model to screen technical résumés, trained on ten years of hiring decisions. It worked as designed — it learned the patterns in the data. The patterns were the problem. Historical hires skewed heavily male, so the model learned that male-associated signals predicted success. It penalized the word "women's" (as in "women's chess club captain") and downgraded graduates of two all-women colleges. Amazon removed explicit gender, and the model found proxies — verbs like "executed" and "captured" that appeared more often on male résumés. They eventually scrapped it. Nothing about the engineering was incompetent. The model faithfully learned a real pattern in real data. **That is precisely the danger: a model optimizing accuracy on historical data will reproduce historical discrimination, and it will do so with the appearance of objectivity.** Responsible AI is not a compliance checkbox appended to a finished project. It is a set of engineering practices — measurement, explanation, and constraint — applied throughout. ##### Where bias comes from Bias enters at identifiable points, and naming them tells you where to look. **Historical bias** — the data accurately reflects a world that is itself unfair. Amazon's case. The data was not wrong; the reality it recorded was discriminatory. **Representation bias** — some groups are underrepresented in training data. Facial recognition systems trained predominantly on light-skinned faces perform substantially worse on dark-skinned ones, a disparity documented extensively in the Gender Shades research. **Measurement bias** — the proxy you measure differs from what you care about. "Arrests" is not "crimes committed"; "healthcare costs incurred" is not "health needs," and a widely-used US healthcare algorithm underserved Black patients precisely because it used cost as a proxy for need. **Aggregation bias** — one model applied to groups with genuinely different underlying relationships, performing well on average and poorly for some. **Deployment bias** — the model is used differently from how it was designed. A risk score built for resource allocation becomes a sentencing input. The critical point for engineers: **removing the sensitive attribute does not remove bias.** Postcode correlates with caste and religion in India, and with race in the US. Name correlates with ethnicity. Purchase history correlates with gender. The model finds the proxies. ##### Measuring fairness You cannot address what you do not measure. Start by computing metrics **per group**: ```python import pandas as pd from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix def fairness_report(y_true, y_pred, y_prob, sensitive_attr) -> pd.DataFrame: """Per-group performance — the foundation of any fairness audit.""" rows = [] for group in sorted(pd.Series(sensitive_attr).unique()): mask = sensitive_attr == group tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true[mask], y_pred[mask]).ravel() rows.append({ "group": group, "n": int(mask.sum()), "selection_rate": (tp + fp) / mask.sum(), # positive prediction rate "tpr": tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) else 0, # recall / sensitivity "fpr": fp / (fp + tn) if (fp + tn) else 0, "precision": tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) else 0, "base_rate": y_true[mask].mean(), # actual positive rate }) return pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4) report = fairness_report(y_test, y_pred, y_prob, X_test["gender"]) print(report) ``` Three formal criteria, and they are worth knowing by name: **Demographic parity** — equal selection rates across groups. `P(ŷ=1|A=a)` is the same for all `a`. Appropriate when you believe the base rates *should* be equal and any difference reflects historical injustice. **Equalized odds** — equal true positive and false positive rates. The model is equally accurate for everyone. Usually the right target for prediction tasks. **Predictive parity** — equal precision. A score of 0.8 means the same thing for everyone. Here is the uncomfortable finding that any honest treatment must include: **when base rates genuinely differ between groups, these criteria are mathematically incompatible.** You cannot satisfy demographic parity and equalized odds and predictive parity simultaneously. This was the core of the ProPublica–Northpointe dispute over the COMPAS recidivism tool: ProPublica showed unequal false positive rates, Northpointe showed equal precision, and **both were correct**. The engineering consequence is that fairness is not a metric you optimize. It is a **choice you make explicitly**, justify, and document. ```python def check_disparate_impact(report: pd.DataFrame) -> dict: """The four-fifths rule — a common regulatory heuristic.""" rates = report.set_index("group")["selection_rate"] ratio = rates.min() / rates.max() return { "disparate_impact_ratio": round(float(ratio), 3), "passes_four_fifths_rule": bool(ratio >= 0.8), "advantaged": rates.idxmax(), "disadvantaged": rates.idxmin(), } ``` Fairlearn provides these metrics plus mitigation algorithms; AIF360 offers a broader set. Both are worth knowing, but the per-group table above catches most problems and takes ten lines. ##### Explainability with SHAP Lundberg and Lee (2017) unified several explanation methods under **SHAP**, based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory. It answers: how much did each feature contribute to *this specific prediction*, relative to the average prediction? ```python import shap explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model) # fast path for tree ensembles shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_test) # Global: which features matter overall, and in which direction shap.summary_plot(shap_values, X_test, feature_names=feature_names) # Local: why THIS applicant was rejected idx = 42 shap.force_plot(explainer.expected_value, shap_values[idx], X_test.iloc[idx]) ``` The **local explanation** is what regulated domains require. Under GDPR's provisions on automated decision-making, and increasingly under sector rules elsewhere, a person affected by an automated decision may be entitled to an explanation. "The model said so" is not one. ```python def explain_decision(model, explainer, row, feature_names, top_n=5) -> str: """Human-readable explanation for a single prediction.""" sv = explainer.shap_values(row.values.reshape(1, -1))[0] contributions = sorted(zip(feature_names, sv, row.values), key=lambda x: abs(x[1]), reverse=True)[:top_n] lines = [f"Prediction: {model.predict_proba(row.values.reshape(1,-1))[0,1]:.1%}", f"Baseline: {explainer.expected_value:.1%}", "", "Key factors:"] for name, contrib, value in contributions: direction = "increased" if contrib > 0 else "decreased" lines.append(f" {name} = {value}: {direction} risk by {abs(contrib):.3f}") return "\n".join(lines) ``` **LIME** is the alternative — it fits a simple interpretable model locally around one prediction. Faster than exact SHAP and less theoretically grounded; useful for text and images. Three cautions worth stating. SHAP explains **what the model did, not what is true** — a model relying on a spurious correlation gets a confident, accurate SHAP explanation of that spurious reliance. With **correlated features**, contributions split arbitrarily between them. And explanation is not justification: showing that postcode drove a rejection explains the mechanism without making it acceptable. ##### Privacy Four practices, in rough order of how often they are neglected. **Data minimization** — collect only what you need. The safest data is data you never held. Before adding a feature, ask whether the accuracy gain justifies the privacy cost and the breach exposure. **Anonymization is harder than it looks.** Removing names is not anonymization. Sweeney's well-known result showed that ZIP code, birth date and sex uniquely identify roughly 87% of the US population. **k-anonymity** requires each record to be indistinguishable from at least k−1 others: ```python def check_k_anonymity(df: pd.DataFrame, quasi_identifiers: list[str], k: int = 5): """Find combinations of quasi-identifiers that uniquely identify people.""" counts = df.groupby(quasi_identifiers).size() violations = counts[counts < k] return { "min_group_size": int(counts.min()), "satisfies_k_anonymity": bool(counts.min() >= k), "vulnerable_records": int(violations.sum()), } ``` **Differential privacy** adds calibrated noise so that no individual's inclusion measurably changes the output — the strongest formal guarantee, at some cost to accuracy. **Regulatory obligations** apply regardless of technique. India's DPDP Act and the EU's GDPR require a lawful basis, purpose limitation, storage limitation, and honouring deletion requests. That last one has a concrete engineering implication: **you must know every place a person's data was copied to**, including training sets. ##### Transparency and accountability **Model cards** document a model the way a datasheet documents a component: ```markdown # Model Card: Loan Default Predictor v2.1 ## Intended use Flag applications for additional human review. **Not** for automated rejection. ## Training data 84,000 applications, Jan 2023 – Dec 2025, Indian retail lending. Default rate 6.2%. Applicants under 21 excluded (insufficient data). ## Performance Overall AUC 0.87 (n=12,000 holdout). | Group | n | AUC | TPR | FPR | Selection rate | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Urban | 8,400 | 0.89 | 0.74 | 0.11 | 0.24 | | Rural | 3,600 | 0.81 | 0.61 | 0.14 | 0.31 | **Known disparity:** TPR is 13 points lower for rural applicants, likely from underrepresentation and thinner credit-bureau coverage. Mitigation: rural applications above 0.4 route to manual review rather than the 0.6 default. ## Limitations - Trained on a period of stable interest rates; behaviour under rate shocks unknown. - Not validated for self-employed applicants (4% of training data). - Degrades on applicants with under 6 months of credit history. ## Ethical considerations Postcode was excluded despite predictive value, as it proxies for community composition. Reviewed by the credit risk committee, 14 March 2026. ``` That **known disparity** section is what distinguishes an honest model card from marketing. Documenting a limitation you could not fully solve, along with the operational mitigation, is more credible and more useful than claiming none exists. **Accountability** means naming a human owner for every deployed model, keeping an audit log of consequential decisions, and defining an escalation path for people who wish to contest an outcome. ##### Regulation The landscape is consolidating around risk-tiered approaches. **The EU AI Act** classifies systems by risk: *unacceptable* uses are banned (social scoring, most real-time biometric identification in public); *high-risk* uses — employment, credit, education, law enforcement — require conformity assessment, documentation, human oversight and logging; *limited-risk* systems need transparency (users must know they are interacting with AI). **India's DPDP Act 2023** governs personal data processing, with consent requirements and data-principal rights including correction and erasure. **Sector rules** often bind more tightly than general AI regulation — RBI guidance for Indian lending, HIPAA for US healthcare, ECOA and FCRA for US credit. The practical implication: **if your model affects someone's access to employment, credit, housing, education or healthcare, assume you are in a high-risk category** and build documentation, human oversight and audit logging in from the start. Retrofitting them is far harder. ##### A responsible deployment checklist ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Before building] --> B[Who could this harm?
What is the worst outcome?] B --> C[Do we need this data?
Lawful basis?] C --> D[During development] D --> E[Per-group performance
+ representation audit] E --> F[Explainability:
SHAP global + local] F --> G{Disparity found?} G -->|yes| H[Mitigate: rebalance,
constrain, adjust threshold] H --> E G -->|no or documented| I[Before deployment] I --> J[Model card + named owner
+ human oversight path] J --> K[Audit logging
+ contest mechanism] K --> L[After deployment] L --> M[Monitor per-group metrics
not just overall] M -->|disparity emerges| H ``` The checklist in words, staged: **Before building** — Who could be harmed, and how badly? Is ML the right tool, or would a transparent rule be better? Do we have a lawful basis for this data? **During development** — Are all relevant groups adequately represented? What are the per-group metrics? Which fairness criterion applies, and why? What do SHAP explanations reveal about which features drive decisions? **Before deployment** — Is there a model card? A named owner? A human review path for consequential decisions? Audit logging? A way for someone to contest an outcome? **After deployment** — Are per-group metrics monitored, not just aggregate accuracy? Is there a scheduled fairness re-audit? A rollback path? ##### Mitigation techniques Interventions apply at three stages: **Pre-processing** — rebalance the training data, reweight samples, or remove proxy features. Simple and often effective. **In-processing** — train with a fairness constraint: ```python from fairlearn.reductions import ExponentiatedGradient, EqualizedOdds mitigated = ExponentiatedGradient( estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), constraints=EqualizedOdds(difference_bound=0.05), ) mitigated.fit(X_train, y_train, sensitive_features=A_train) ``` **Post-processing** — adjust decision thresholds per group to equalize the chosen criterion. The simplest lever, and legally sensitive in some jurisdictions since it means treating groups differently by design. Every mitigation trades something. Enforcing equalized odds usually costs a little aggregate accuracy. **That trade-off should be a documented decision, made by people accountable for the outcome — not a default chosen silently by an engineer.** ##### Common mistakes - **Assuming that removing the sensitive attribute removes bias** — proxies remain. - **Reporting only aggregate metrics**, hiding severe group disparities. - **Treating fairness as one metric** when the criteria are mathematically incompatible. - **Explaining without auditing** — SHAP tells you what the model does, not whether it is fair. - **Anonymizing by dropping names**, ignoring quasi-identifier re-identification. - **No model card**, so limitations are undocumented and unknown to users. - **No human review path** for consequential automated decisions. - **Monitoring aggregate accuracy only**, missing disparities that emerge post-deployment. - **Treating ethics as a final review** rather than a development practice. - **No named owner** for a deployed model that affects people. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: use **SHAP or LIME to explain a model's predictions**, and **audit a model for bias across a sensitive attribute**. Do both on the same model, because the combination is where insight comes from — SHAP shows you *which* feature drives decisions, and the fairness table shows you *whether* that produces disparate outcomes. A feature with high SHAP importance that also correlates with a protected attribute is exactly what you are looking for. The mini project is a **fairness and explainability report** for one of your earlier models, identifying bias and **proposing mitigations**. Structure it as a model card. Include the per-group metrics table, the disparate impact ratio, SHAP summary and one worked local explanation, and — critically — a section on limitations you could not resolve. That honesty is what makes such a report credible. For the assignment, **describe a real case where ML bias caused harm and outline detection and mitigation steps**. The Amazon hiring model, the COMPAS dispute, and the US healthcare algorithm that used cost as a proxy for need are all well-documented. Pick one, explain the specific mechanism — what the model optimized, what the data encoded, why the sensitive attribute's removal did not help — then give concrete steps: per-group evaluation before deployment, representation auditing of the training data, proxy detection, a chosen and justified fairness criterion, human oversight for consequential decisions, and ongoing per-group monitoring. ##### Key takeaways - Models faithfully learn historical patterns, including discriminatory ones — removing the sensitive attribute does not help, because proxies remain. - Measure per-group performance, not aggregate accuracy; the standard fairness criteria are mathematically incompatible when base rates differ, so the choice must be explicit and justified. - SHAP provides local explanations required for contesting automated decisions, but it explains what the model does rather than whether that is right. - Minimize data collected, recognize that dropping names is not anonymization, and design for deletion requests from the start. - Ship a model card with per-group metrics and honest limitations, name an owner, provide human review for consequential decisions, and monitor disparities after deployment.
